_why: PROJECT ANNOTATIONS the audit pipeline does not produce, applied by
scripts/generate-statute-tables.mjs on top of audited rows.
`residual` is the one that matters. A residual clause applies to whatever
the rest of the section does not reach, so any sentence giving it a dollar
floor asserts something about every other paragraph. All three errors that
shipped on the grand theft page were exactly that sentence, and
check-claims.mts catches them ONLY via rows flagged residual.
The build/audit schema has no residual field: auditors describe the clause
in `trigger` prose instead. Prose does not arm a guard. Without this file
the generated table would drop the flag and the residual rule would go
quiet while still appearing to run, which is precisely the failure mode
this project already hit once with the completeness flag.
A cite listed here that matches no row is a hard error, not a warning, so
a renumbered subsection cannot silently disarm the rule.
`amountUnit` says what min and max COUNT. The schema stores dollars, drug
weights, pill counts, and victim counts in the same two numeric fields, so
the amount rules in check-claims.mts will happily compare a $1,000 fine to
a 1,000 GRAM trafficking threshold and report a wrong degree. Probed and
confirmed: degreesAt("893.13", 1000) returns two felony degrees off a
weight ladder.
There is deliberately NO DEFAULT. A statute with bounded rows that is a
page's primary statute must declare its unit or the gate fails, because a
default of usd would let the next quantity-graded statute through in
silence, and silence is the failure mode this whole file exists to stop.
Values: "usd" runs the amount rules; anything else disables them for that
statute and says so out loud on every run.
CONVENTION, settled 2026-08-14 after two agents disagreed about it inside
a data field: A COUNT OF PRIOR CONVICTIONS LIVES IN TRIGGER TEXT, WITH min
AND max NULL, AND scope "prior". min and max are thresholds of the OFFENSE
CONDUCT, a dollar value or a quantity of the thing involved. Criminal
history is not conduct, and putting a count of priors in min would make
rowsAt() answer a question about money or weight with a row about a record.
F.S. 812.014(3)(c) and 18 U.S.C. 2251(e) are both recorded this way.
WHERE TWO TIERS SHARE A CITE, THE CITE IS DISAMBIGUATED IN PARENTHESES
rather than left identical: "18 U.S.C. 2251(e) (one prior conviction)" and
"... (two or more prior convictions)". An auditor reading two rows with the
same cite, degree, scope and null bounds cannot tell them apart at a glance
even when their triggers and quotes differ, and check-claims matches rows
by cite, so identical cites also collapse two tiers into one lookup.
AND NO FIELD CARRIES ARGUMENT. A trigger describes the provision. It is not
the place to answer an auditor, justify a convention, or record a decision;
a build shipped triggers reading "I therefore decline the audit's proposal",
which would have rendered as legal description if anything consumed it.

812.014.note: All 17 bounded rows are property values in dollars. Theft of any property not specified in subsection (2) is the residual: its floor is wherever the other paragraphs stop, so it has none of its own.

817.034.note: Aggregate value of the scheme, and per-act value for communications fraud. Dollars throughout.

896.101.note: Financial transaction totals in dollars. (5)(a) reads 'exceeding $300', which the row's own trigger text records as exclusive while the typed min could not express it: the table was audited before minExclusive existed. Transcribed here rather than left in prose, because $300 exactly is a real boundary a page could state wrongly.

841.note: AMOUNT RULES OFF. All 17 bounded rows are drug weights in GRAMS, and the numbers look exactly like money: 1000 for a kilogram of heroin, 5000 for cocaine, 280 for cocaine base, 100 for PCP. A page saying a $5,000 fine on this charge would be compared against the 5,000 GRAM cocaine threshold. This is the same collision that took 893.13 out of the amount rules, and it is worse here because the federal page discusses fines and forfeiture in the same breath as quantities.

1030.note: AMOUNT RULES OFF. Two of the three bounded rows are dollars, (c)(2)(B)(iii) at 5000 and (c)(4)(A)(i)(I) at 5000, but (c)(4)(A)(i)(VI) is a count of PROTECTED COMPUTERS at 10, not money. A dollar claim at $10 would meet the computer-count row. The two dollar figures also differ in kind: (c)(2)(B)(iii) reads 'exceeds $5,000' and carries minExclusive, while (c)(4)(A)(i)(I) reads 'aggregating at least $5,000' and is inclusive. And the $5,000 inside (a)(4) is a CARVE-OUT that removes conduct from the offense rather than a floor, so it is recorded nowhere in min at all.

896.104.note: Financial transaction values in dollars, in the same three-tier shape as 896.101(5). Note the builder encoded the two strict thresholds as 300.01 and 10000.01 rather than as a round bound with minExclusive; the arithmetic comes out right at $300 and $10,000 either way, but a future re-audit should normalize it so the convention matches 896.101(5)(a).

817.568.note: AMOUNT RULES OFF, and this is the clearest case for the whole mechanism. Paragraphs (2)(b) and (2)(c) each carry TWO independent prongs sharing one pair of numeric fields: a dollar prong ($5,000 or more, $50,000 or more, $100,000 or more) and a person-count prong (10 to 20 persons, 20 to 30, 30 or more). The ranges overlap in the small numbers, so a sentence about $15 would be compared against the 10-to-20 PERSON row and answered with a felony degree. No page may have its dollar claims about this statute machine-checked.

1956.note: AMOUNT RULES OFF. The three bounded rows are dollars, but none of them grades an offense: (c)(7)(D) and (c)(7)(G) are predicate-qualifying thresholds inside the definition of specified unlawful activity, and (f)(2) is the extraterritorial jurisdiction threshold. Comparing a sentence's dollar figure against them would answer a grading question with a jurisdiction rule.

893.13.note: AMOUNT RULES OFF. Bounds are grams throughout, except 893.13(8)(d)'s $1,000 payment prong. This is the collision that prompted the mechanism: degreesAt('893.13', 1000) returns two felony degrees off the weight ladder, so a $1,000 fine mentioned on a drug page would have been checked against 'more than 10 grams'.

322.2615.note: AMOUNT RULES OFF. Every bound is 0.08, a blood or breath alcohol level, and the provisions are administrative suspension rules rather than criminal grading.
